common_name: De La Mina Verbena (Cedros Island Baja California Native Verbena)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or container plants in spring or fall into lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; this Baja California island native resents summer irrigation once established and performs best on a lean diet.

directions: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot inland climates. De La Mina forms a rounded, woody-based mound of soft gray-green foliage covered almost year-round in coastal California with dense spikes of rich violet-purple flowers that draw butterflies and hoverflies in steady numbers. Native to Cedros Island off Baja California, it tolerates both coastal fog and dry heat but declines quickly in heavy clay or where summer water lingers around the crown. Shear lightly after the main flush of bloom to keep the habit tidy and encourage repeat flowering through the following season.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall onto rocky or gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; natural winter cold and moisture cycles improve germination the following spring.

directions: Direct sow or set out small transplants into rocky, gravelly, or sandy well-drained soil in full sun. This compact, wiry southwestern native produces slender spikes of small pale lavender to white flowers from late spring through fall and is well adapted to the dry rocky slopes, canyons, and roadsides of the desert Southwest. It tolerates extended drought once established and needs no supplemental irrigation in adapted sites, but will not persist in heavy or poorly drained soil. Its low, open habit suits rock gardens and naturalistic xeric plantings rather than formal beds.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into moist, average garden soil in full sun; established plants tolerate occasional flooding and brief drought equally well.

directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun; seashore vervain is an upright, branching species widely naturalized along coastal flats, ditches, and disturbed open ground from California to the Gulf Coast and Hawaii. Slim spikes of small lavender-blue flowers appear from summer into fall and attract a steady stream of small butterflies and native bees. It tolerates both brief waterlogging and dry spells once established, making it useful in low spots that other verbenas reject, and it self-sows readily where conditions suit it. Cut plants back after the first bloom flush to keep growth compact and encourage continued flowering.

planting.note: Direct sow at or just after last frost into dry, well-drained, often calcareous soil in full sun; thin seedlings to allow the low, spreading clumps room to fill in.

directions: Direct sow into dry, rocky, or caliche-heavy well-drained soil in full sun. Native to the limestone prairies and open woodland edges of central and south Texas, fan-leaf vervain produces low mounds of finely divided foliage topped by rounded clusters of small lavender-pink flowers from spring through fall, with a strong flush after rain. It is highly drought tolerant once established and performs reliably in the thin, alkaline soils that limit many garden perennials. Where winters are mild it behaves as a short-lived perennial, reseeding to maintain a colony even if individual plants decline.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center - Verbena plicata

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into dry, well-drained desert soil in full sun, or set out transplants in spring after danger of hard frost has passed.

directions: Plant in dry, well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; mint-leaf vervain is an upright southwestern native of washes, roadsides, and disturbed desert ground, bearing slender spikes of small lavender flowers over aromatic, mint-scented foliage from summer into fall. It is extremely drought tolerant once established and typically needs no supplemental water beyond infrequent deep soakings during extended dry spells. Cut stems back hard in late winter to refresh the clump, since older growth becomes woody and sparse over time. Its understated flowers nonetheless draw small native bees and butterflies in arid gardens.

planting.note: Set out transplants after last frost into average, well-drained soil in full sun; this low spreading South American native roots readily at the nodes and fills in quickly.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Lilac Spires forms a dense, ground-hugging mat of small toothed leaves studded with pale lilac-blue flowers from spring through fall. Stems root wherever they touch soil, letting a single plant spread steadily to cover bare ground, cascade over walls, or soften path edges within a season. It tolerates heat and drought well once established but flowers most heavily with occasional deep watering during the hottest weeks of summer. Shear lightly after the first flush of bloom to keep growth tight and encourage continued flowering into fall.

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated transplants after last frost into well-drained soil in full sun; part of the Tapien series bred for a tight, finely cut-leaved habit and good mildew resistance.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Tapien Pink spreads into a dense, low groundcover of small, finely dissected leaves covered in clear pink flower clusters from spring through frost. Its tight, uniform habit and improved resistance to powdery mildew make it a dependable choice for hanging baskets, window boxes, and sunny groundcover plantings where older seed verbenas often decline by midsummer. It tolerates heat and drought well once roots are established, and a light shearing after the first bloom flush keeps the mat dense and encourages fresh flowering.

common_name: Tapien Blue Violet Verbena (Fine-Textured Spreading Verbena)

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated transplants after last frost into well-drained soil in full sun, spacing to allow the trailing stems room to knit together.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Tapien Blue Violet forms a dense, finely textured mat of deeply cut foliage smothered in rich violet-blue flower clusters from spring through frost. Its compact, uniform spreading habit and solid resistance to powdery mildew carry it through humid summers that often disfigure older trailing verbena types. Use it in hanging baskets, mixed containers, or as a sun-loving groundcover; established plantings shrug off heat and short dry spells with only occasional deep watering. A light shearing after the initial flush renews density and bloom.

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated transplants after last frost into well-drained soil in full sun; the soft salmon color of this Tapien selection combines well with warm-toned companion plantings.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Tapien Salmon spreads into a low, dense mat of fine, cut-leaf foliage topped with clusters of soft salmon-orange flowers from spring through frost. Like the rest of the series, it holds its tight habit without becoming leggy and resists the powdery mildew that often limits older trailing verbena selections through a humid summer. It thrives in hanging baskets and sunny groundcover plantings, tolerating heat and brief drought well once established, and benefits from a light shearing after the first bloom flush to maintain density.

common_name: Tukana Scarlet Verbena (Vigorous Large-Flowered Spreading Verbena)

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated transplants after last frost into well-drained soil in full sun, spacing widely since Tukana selections spread vigorously by season's end.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Tukana Scarlet grows into a vigorous, fast-spreading groundcover carrying large clusters of bright scarlet-red flowers continuously from spring through frost. Bred for larger flower trusses and sturdier stems than many older verbena series, it fills landscape beds, large containers, and raised planters quickly while holding up well to summer heat and humidity. Established plantings are drought tolerant and benefit from an occasional shearing back to refresh growth and keep the center of the planting from thinning out by late summer.

common_name: Quartz Burgundy Verbena (Dwarf Mildew-Resistant Bedding Verbena)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperatures, or set out purchased transplants after danger of frost; part of the compact, early-flowering Quartz series bred for uniform bedding display.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Quartz Burgundy forms tight, compact mounds covered in deep wine-red flower clusters from shortly after transplanting through frost. Its dwarf, uniform habit and improved tolerance of powdery mildew make it well suited to mass bedding displays, edging, and containers where even height and season-long color matter. It flowers earlier from seed than many older verbena types and holds up well through summer heat with regular watering, needing only light deadheading to maintain a tidy appearance.

common_name: Quartz Pink Verbena (Dwarf Mildew-Resistant Bedding Verbena)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperatures, or set out purchased transplants after danger of frost; the Quartz series was bred for compact, early, uniform bedding performance.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Quartz Pink produces dense, compact mounds of clear pink flower clusters from shortly after transplanting through frost. The tight, even habit and resistance to powdery mildew that typify the Quartz series suit it to mass plantings, edging, and container combinations where uniform height and continuous bloom are priorities. It flowers reliably from an earlier seed-grown stage than many traditional verbenas and performs well through summer heat with regular watering and occasional deadheading.

common_name: Babylon Blue Verbena (Compact Large-Flowered Bedding Verbena)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperatures, or set out purchased transplants after danger of frost; Babylon series plants branch freely without pinching for an early, full look.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Babylon Blue grows into a compact, naturally branching mound covered with large clusters of rich blue-violet flowers from shortly after transplanting until frost. Bred to fill out quickly without pinching, it produces a full, well-rounded plant that suits mixed containers, window boxes, and bedding display equally well. It tolerates heat better than many older seed verbenas and continues flowering through summer with regular watering and light deadheading of spent flower heads.

common_name: Babylon Scarlet Verbena (Compact Large-Flowered Bedding Verbena)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperatures, or set out purchased transplants after danger of frost; branches freely without pinching for a full early display.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Babylon Scarlet forms a compact, freely branching mound topped with large clusters of vivid scarlet-red flowers from shortly after transplanting until frost. Its naturally full habit fills containers and bedding rows quickly without the pinching older seed verbena types often require. Plants hold up well through summer heat and humidity with regular watering, and light deadheading of spent flower clusters keeps the display fresh into fall.
